html_en:
The AI industry is living through a profound crisis of shared reality — where a tiny sliver of professionals witness capabilities that the rest of the world can barely imagine, and the gap is only widening.

The Funnel: How AI Capability Is Experienced Across Humanity

The most resonant piece of writing circulating today comes from Andrej Karpathy, who revisited a tweet from April and found it had only grown more urgent. His framing of a "capability funnel" has captured exactly the strange, vertiginous moment we're in.

"Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search... Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math & code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt." — @karpathy

The bottom of the funnel is the most striking part. Karpathy describes roughly 5,000 people — 0.00006% of humanity — with access to truly frontier-grade internal systems:

"It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind." — @karpathy

Aaron Levie offered perhaps the most practically-minded response, noting that even for enterprises ready to embrace agent swarms, there's a long road ahead:

"There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work — beyond software and AI research — to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to be integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off." — @levie

Garry Tan took a more bullish, almost evangelical read: "Be part of the 5000 today. It's amazing... Greatest alpha fountain in the history of man."

OpenAI's Codex Rollout Continues — Context Windows Just Got Bigger

While the philosophical debate raged, OpenAI was busy shipping. Thomas Sottiaux has been running what appears to be a daily product update series, and Day 7 brought a meaningful upgrade to GPT-6.1 Sol:

"We have increased default context length for GPT-6.1 Sol to 500k when used through Codex & Work, up from 272k — an ~80% increase. We will go higher in the future, but it helps reduce occurrence of compactions and with tasks that require keeping a lot of context and nuance over periods of time." — @thsottiaux

He also confirmed that long context fees won't apply to GPT-6.1 Sol when drawing from subscription usage — a notable pricing decision designed to reduce friction for power users. And in a candid aside, Sottiaux admitted surprise at user polling results around usage limits, suggesting he expected more appetite for higher limits even at the cost of bringing back usage caps.

The Trust Problem: Human-in-the-Loop Is Still the Default

For all the wonder of agent swarms, practitioners are still wrestling with a basic question: when do you trust the agent enough to let go? Peter Yang surfaced a thoughtful perspective from Micky (@Rasmic), who has taught over 100,000 people to build with AI:

"I'm not at a point where I trust the agent, especially with stuff that people are using. The manual review is like the final step. All the work's done, and I have as much evidence from the agent as possible. With evidence-driven testing, before and after, and even greploop, we're trying to build trust. The agent presents evidence: This is the work that's done, and this is why it's good." — Micky (@Rasmic), via @petergyang

Watch/Listen: Micky's full 4-step agentic workflow

This tension — between the breathtaking capability Karpathy describes and the very human instinct to verify — is arguably the defining challenge of applied AI right now. @trq212 put it well, echoing Terence Tao: "A key signal of intelligence is communication. We should strive to make products and models that build understanding with humans instead of disintermediating them."

The Hardware Race Underneath It All

Today's episode of No Priors goes deep on the chip infrastructure powering this moment. Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of Fractile, makes the case for why the inference chip landscape — despite its apparent variety — is less differentiated than it looks.

"When you kind of zoom into this seeming embarrassment of riches in the spectrum of what exists today, you see that actually there's a lot of similarity across these platforms. All of these chips have HBM, the same kinds of bets on Tensor Cores to do your matrix multiplications, the same advanced packaging with TSMC." — Walter Goodwin, No Priors

Fractile's bet is to go all the way down the silicon stack — from architecture to physical design — rather than outsourcing the hard parts to ASIC houses like Broadcom. Goodwin's thesis on winning in this market has a clean competitive logic:

"The frontier model for the chip space is: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." — Walter Goodwin, No Priors

Watch/Listen: Frontier Chips for Frontier AI Labs, with Walter Goodwin — No Priors

Brief Notes

Matt Turck offered some historical comfort to anyone anxious about job displacement: "People were punch card operators then they were Lotus Notes admins, then they were Flash developers and Dreamweaver webmasters... and now they're becoming agent managers and harness engineers. It will work out just fine." Reassuring, if you believe the pattern holds.

Garry Tan made a sharp engineering point worth flagging: "Replacing LLM calls with deterministic code is a no brainer and also results in better code that better matches what users want." A useful corrective against reflexive AI-for-everything thinking.

And Guillermo Rauch flagged something that caught his eye on the learning front — "So cool. The future of learning" — though as ever, the most interesting content lives behind the link.
html_zh:
今天的核心主题只有一个：AI能力的认知鸿沟正在急速扩大——从几乎没用过聊天机器人的普通大众，到亲眼目睹"曲线垂直拉升"的少数精英，这个漏斗正在重塑整个行业的格局。

📡 漏斗效应：75亿人与5000人之间的平行宇宙

本周最值得反复阅读的一条推文，来自 Andrej Karpathy。他重新发布了一篇今年四月写的分析，并指出情况已经比当时更为极端。他将全球人口对AI的认知分为四层：

"约60亿人（75%的人口）几乎从未接触过LLM。约10-20亿人（20%）是ChatGPT类产品的随意用户，把它当成更好用的谷歌搜索或写作辅助。我有不少非技术圈的朋友，他们觉得这东西对自己没什么用——这个判断，我认为是合理的。"
— @karpathy

而进入漏斗更深处，画风急剧变化：

"大约有2000万人（0.2%）在数学和代码领域专业使用前沿LLM。他们亲眼看到，以前需要几周甚至几个月才能完成的大型复杂项目，现在可以由智能体用一句提示词完成。不到一年前，我还在手动逐字敲代码。"
— @karpathy

而漏斗的最底端，则近乎科幻：

"大约5000人（0.00006%）可以接触到内部前沿系统。外界已经看到了预告片：数千个智能体协作数周完成软件超级项目，自动发现零日漏洞，以机器速度运行网络攻防，探索新科学，推进数学前沿……而人类的审阅和理解能力正开始落后。"
— @karpathy

Box CEO Aaron Levie 对此做了很好的商业层补充：

"这清晰地展示了AI扩散目前还有多早期。绝大多数人把AI当成聊天机器人用于简单互动，本质上是下一代搜索。这非常有用，但严重低估了AI的完整能力。"
— @levie

YC的 Garry Tan 则毫不掩饰他的兴奋：

"今天就加入那5000人的行列吧。幸运的是，价格会下降，更多人会看到这一切——这是人类历史上最伟大的阿尔法之泉。"
— @garrytan

🛠️ OpenAI Codex产品更新：上下文长度突破与定价调整

在产品层面，OpenAI的 Thomas Sottiaux 连续发布了多条关于Codex的更新，第七天的公告尤为值得关注：

"我们已将GPT-6.1 Sol通过Codex & Work使用时的默认上下文长度增加至50万token，较之前的27.2万提升约80%。这有助于减少压缩发生的频率，并改善需要在长时间内保持大量上下文和细节的任务。这是经过仔细测试后确定的新甜蜜点，最大上下文长度上限为100万token。"
— @thsottiaux

与此同时，他还宣布了一项对重度用户友好的定价政策：

"通过订阅使用GPT-6.1 Sol时，我们不会对长上下文收取额外费用。"
— @thsottiaux

他还透露，关于是否应该以更高的使用量换取时间限制的用户调研结果出乎意料——民意并未如他预想的那样倾向于"2倍用量"方向，这让他感到困惑。产品团队显然仍在摸索订阅价值主张的最优解。

🤝 人机协作：信任、审查与工作流的重新定义

Peter Yang 分享了一段来自教过十万人用AI构建产品的创作者 Micky（@Rasmic）的洞察，直击当前AI工作流的核心矛盾：

"我现在还不到完全信任智能体的阶段，尤其是在别人会用到的东西上。人工审查是最后一步。所有工作都已完成，我从智能体那里获取了尽可能多的证据。通过证据驱动的测试——前后对比，甚至是greploop——我们在努力建立信任。智能体呈现证据：这是已完成的工作，这是它质量过关的原因。对于任何做过一段时间开发的人来说，人工审查可能是你工作中最痛苦的部分。这种方式帮助最小化了这种摩擦。"
— Micky，via @petergyang

这与 @trq212 呼应数学家陶哲轩观点的推文形成有趣的共振：

"我认为陶哲轩的方向是对的，我们不应该满足于一个不透明的超级智能。智能的一个关键信号是沟通能力。我们应该努力打造能与人类建立共同理解的产品和模型，而不是将人类边缘化。"
— @trq212

Garry Tan 则从工程实践角度提出了一个务实原则：

"用确定性代码替换LLM调用是毋庸置疑的正确选择，而且结果往往更好，更符合用户需求。"
— @garrytan

💾 芯片军备竞赛：Fractile的全栈押注

今天的播客值得单独拿出来说。Watch/Listen: No Priors — Frontier Chips for Frontier AI Labs, with Walter Goodwin (Fractile CEO)

Fractile创始人Walter Goodwin描述了当前AI芯片市场一个反直觉的现象：尽管市面上已经有Google TPU、Meta MTIA、Microsoft Maya、OpenAI Jalapeno等琳琅满目的定制芯片，但它们在技术路线上高度雷同——都依赖HBM内存、Tensor Core矩阵运算单元，以及TSMC的先进封装，都通过Broadcom等ASIC代工厂实现。

"当你拆开NVIDIA的系统，里面有六到九颗NVIDIA自研的定制芯片协同工作，才能构建出那样强大的系统。所以差距已经存在了。如果我们能高效地在同一方向上构建自己的应对方案，这将是巨大的优势。"
— Walter Goodwin，No Priors

Fractile的差异化押注在于从架构层一路做到物理设计层的"全栈"路径，核心聚焦于推理速度和内存带宽。Goodwin用一个简洁的竞争逻辑总结了芯片前沿的生存法则：

"芯片领域的前沿模型等价物是：如果你能找到一种方式，在结构上保持三到六个月的领先优势，你就能赢得所有的部署机会。"
— Walter Goodwin，No Priors

在模型能力的漏斗效应之下，还有一场更底层的硬件竞赛正在悄然进行。谁能率先突破推理速度的物理极限，谁就可能重新定义那5000人所能触及的"前沿"边界。

⚡ 快讯速览

职业演化论： Matt Turck 以一句话安抚了所有对AI取代工作的焦虑者——"人们曾是打孔卡操作员，然后是Lotus Notes管理员，然后是Flash开发者和Dreamweaver网站管理员，然后是DevOps工程师和Tableau分析师，现在正在成为智能体管理者和harness工程师。一切都会好起来的。"

学习的未来： Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch 分享了一个AI辅助学习的演示，简短地感叹"学习的未来"——获得了近2700个点赞，引发广泛共鸣。

Gemini的尴尬处境： @zarazhangrui 道出了许多人的心声——"我现在唯一还在用Gemini的地方是Chrome浏览器里。" 这句话不需要任何补充。
